text: Everything so far in this chapter — pipelines, canary, blue-green, automated rollback — operates on deployed code and infrastructure traffic. None of it asks whether users should actually see the new behavior yet. That's a separate question, and feature flags are how you answer it on purpose instead of by accident.

Deploy means new code is now running somewhere in production. Release means users can actually see and use it. In a naive pipeline those happen at the same instant — the moment code deploys, whoever hits it sees the new behavior, whether you meant to show it to them yet or not. That coupling means every single deploy carries release-level risk, with no way to separate the two.

A feature flag breaks that coupling with a runtime check, usually backed by a service like LaunchDarkly or the open-source Unleash, or built against the vendor-neutral OpenFeature standard. In code, that's a call like flags dot isEnabled, checked per request. The new checkout code can be fully deployed to a hundred percent of production servers while that flag stays off for every single user — deploying it and turning it on are now two separate actions.

A real targeting rule shows what that buys you: serve the new behavior to the internal segment, and to five percent of users in a rollout bucket, by default false for everyone else. Notice this is the same percentage-rollout idea as a canary, but it's happening at the application layer, based on who the user is — not at the infrastructure layer, based on which pods happen to receive the request.

That gives you three things a rollback alone can't: deploying continuously without forcing a user-facing change every time, targeting a release to a specific segment or account independent of infrastructure, and an instant kill switch — flipping a feature off with no redeploy and no pipeline run at all.

None of this chapter's tools can tell you how users actually behave once a feature is fully visible — that's exactly why release stays its own deliberate decision, made after deploy, built on top of the pipeline, traffic-shifting, and automated-analysis mechanics you've now seen across this entire chapter.
